Act of Classes
akt ov klas'ez
n. (the Act of the Scottish Parliament of January 1649 excluding Engagers and Malignants from public trust)
class, from Latin classis, a division or rank; the Act sorted the excluded into four classes by degree of guilt.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Act of Classes was passed by the Scottish Parliament in January 1649, in the brief ascendancy of the strict Covenanting party after the defeat of the Engagement. It excluded from all public office — parliament, council, army, burgh magistracy — everyone who had taken part in the Engagement of 1648 to rescue Charles I on terms the Church judged unlawful, or in Montrose's royalist war, or had otherwise acted against the Covenant; and it sorted them into four classes according to the degree of their offence, with periods of exclusion from one year to life, each requiring evidence of repentance before restoration. It was the high-water mark of the attempt to make a nation's public life answer to a church's judgment of character. It also left Scotland short of experienced officers when Cromwell crossed the border, which is precisely the pressure that produced the Public Resolutions; Parliament repealed it in June 1651. “He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house” (Psa 101:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a class as a rank or order of persons, and to exclude as to thrust out, to hinder from entrance or participation.

expand to see more

CLASS, n. An order or rank of persons; a number of persons in society supposed to have the same position.

EXCLUDE', v. To thrust out; to hinder from entrance or admission; to debar from participation.

MALIG'NANT, n. In English and Scottish history, a name given by the Covenanters to the royalists.

REPEAL', v. To recall, as a deed or law; to revoke; to abrogate by authority.

Modern Corruption

Four classes of exclusion from public trust, passed in 1649 and repealed in 1651.

expand to see more

The Act of Classes is a standing exhibit for the claim that Reformed political theology ends in theocratic exclusion: a church deciding who may hold office in a commonwealth. The dictionary neither defends the Act as a model nor accepts the caricature. Scotland was a covenanted nation by its own parliament's deed, and the Act applied a condition the nation had sworn to; its practical fault was not that it took public faithfulness seriously but that it bound a kingdom's whole administrative capacity to a classification that could not be revised under pressure except by repeal.

The principle to recover is that public trust is rightly conditioned on character, and that the conditioning is a sound instinct even when a particular statute embodying it is clumsy. David's charter for his own household is exclusionary on exactly that ground: “He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house: he that telleth lies shall not tarry in my sight” (Psa 101:7). Nehemiah's reform was of the same kind: “Thus cleansed I them from all strangers, and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites” (Neh 13:30).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Usage

"“He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house” (Psa 101:7) — the Act's own principle."

"“Thus cleansed I them from all strangers” (Neh 13:30) — the precedent its framers cited."

"“the hand of the princes and rulers hath been chief in this trespass” (Ezr 9:2) — why rulers were classed first."
